title: “PASSIONS OF THE FLESH” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs:
“PASSIONS OF THE FLESH” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS
You can look disciplined on the outside, know your Bible, attend church, and still be quietly obeying desires that are pulling your heart away from Jesus. Scripture has a name for that war—and understanding it may change the way you fight.
There are sins everybody can see.
Then there are desires nobody sees until they have already begun rearranging your soul.
The private resentment you keep feeding.
The fantasy you keep returning to.
The approval you cannot stop craving.
The anger that feels too satisfying to surrender.
The money you need because somehow “enough” never feels like enough.
The secret comparison.
The hunger to be admired.
The appetite that keeps whispering, Just once more.
And perhaps the most frightening part is this:
You can become very good at looking spiritually alive while something underneath is slowly learning to live without surrendering to Jesus.
That is why Peter wrote words that deserve more than a hurried reading:
“Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul.”
—1 Peter 2:11
The Greek is startling.
Peter speaks of τῶν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν (tōn sarkikōn epithymiōn)—“fleshly desires” or “desires belonging to the flesh.”
Then he says these desires στρατεύονται κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς (strateuontai kata tēs psychēs).
They “wage war against the soul.”
That verb, strateuontai, comes from the language of military service and warfare.
Peter does not describe sinful desire as a harmless personality quirk.
He describes a battle.
And suddenly the struggle becomes much more serious.
That thing you keep excusing may be fighting for territory.
That appetite you keep entertaining may not intend to remain an appetite.
It wants obedience.
It wants repetition.
It wants habit.
Eventually, it wants a throne.
But before we misunderstand Peter, we need to clarify something Christians have sometimes handled badly:
Your physical body is not the enemy.
Christianity does not teach that matter is evil, that normal bodily existence is shameful, or that holiness means becoming less human.
God created human beings physically and called His creation “very good” (Genesis 1:31).
Jesus Christ truly came in the flesh (John 1:14).
Jesus ate.
Jesus slept.
Jesus became tired.
Jesus wept.
Jesus experienced anguish.
Jesus attended a wedding feast.
Jesus was tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
And Christian hope is not ultimately escape from embodiment but resurrection.
So when Scripture speaks about “the flesh,” we cannot automatically translate it as “the physical body.”

The Greek word σάρξ (sarx) can literally mean flesh or bodily existence depending on context. But especially in Paul, it can also describe fallen humanity operating independently of God—the human person under sin’s corrupting influence.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because otherwise Christianity becomes a war against being human.
The Gospel is something far more beautiful.
It is God redeeming fallen human beings through Jesus Christ.
Paul writes:
—Galatians 5:16
Again, the Greek word for desire is ἐπιθυμία (epithymia).
Interestingly, epithymia does not automatically mean something evil merely because it is a strong desire. Context determines its moral character.
Jesus Himself says in Luke 22:15:
ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπεθύμησα
(epithymia epethymēsa)
Literally, an emphatic expression of intense desire: “I have earnestly desired” to eat this Passover with His disciples.
So desire itself is not automatically sinful.
That changes the conversation.
The problem is not that you desire.
God created human beings capable of desire.
You desire food because bodies need nourishment.
You desire intimacy because human beings were made relational.
You desire rest because you are not God.
You desire significance because your life actually matters.
You desire justice because evil really is evil.
You desire beauty because creation bears witness to its Creator.
Sin takes desires and disorders them.
It takes hunger and turns it into enslavement.
It takes sexuality and detaches it from God's purposes.
It takes rest and turns it into laziness.
It takes stewardship and turns it into greed.
It takes healthy concern about reputation and turns it into an addiction to human approval.
It takes righteous anger and corrupts it into hatred.
It takes the desire to accomplish something meaningful and transforms it into a desperate need to prove that you matter.
Sometimes the most dangerous desires are not desires for obviously evil things.
They are desires for good things that have become ultimate things.
And anything you cannot surrender to Jesus is beginning to tell you who your real master is.
That is why the “passions of the flesh” are much bigger than sexual temptation.
Sexual immorality certainly belongs to the biblical picture. Paul explicitly includes it when describing the works of the flesh.
But look at what else appears beside it:
“sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these.”
—Galatians 5:19–21
Read that again slowly.
Jealousy.
Anger.
Rivalries.
Division.
Envy.
Suddenly “flesh” is no longer somebody else’s scandal.
It is possible to avoid drunkenness while being drunk on attention.
Possible to avoid adultery while secretly worshiping admiration.
Possible to condemn somebody else’s sexual sin while feeding your own bitterness every evening.
Possible to carry a Bible while carrying unforgiveness.
Possible to defend sound doctrine with an ego that desperately needs to win.
Possible to sing worship songs on Sunday while spending Monday through Saturday consumed with envy.
Possible even to do ministry while craving applause more than the glory of Christ.
The flesh can wear church clothes.
That is what makes it dangerous.
Sometimes rebellion does not scream.
Sometimes it serves.
Sometimes it posts Bible verses.
Sometimes it knows Christian vocabulary.
Sometimes it says all the correct things while quietly asking:
Did they notice me?
And this is where Scripture stops being something we use to diagnose everybody else.
It becomes a mirror.
Maybe your struggle is lust.
Maybe pornography has trained your imagination to treat people made in God's image as objects for consumption.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you promised God after the last time that it really was the last time.
Then loneliness came.
Stress came.
The phone was nearby.
And the old pathway opened again.
Maybe your flesh speaks differently.
Maybe it says:
You deserve to stay angry.
They hurt you.
They never apologized properly.
So you replay the conversation.
You rehearse what you should have said.
You imagine them finally suffering enough to understand what they did.
And bitterness begins masquerading as justice.
Maybe yours says:
Make more money. Then you will finally feel secure.
So the target moves.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Maybe it says:
Make people admire you.
So every compliment becomes food and every criticism becomes a wound.
Maybe it says:
Be needed.
And suddenly even helping people becomes a way of proving your worth.
Maybe it says:
Control everything.
Because surrender feels terrifying.
Different appetite.
Same throne.
This is why Paul gives us one of Scripture’s most important distinctions:
“For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh.”
—Galatians 5:17
There is conflict.
And if you belong to Christ and still experience that conflict, the existence of temptation does not by itself prove that Christ has abandoned you.
Temptation is not identical to surrender.
Jesus was tempted without sin.
The decisive question is not simply, What temptation appeared?
It is:
What am I doing with it?
Am I feeding it?
Protecting it?
Planning around it?
Making excuses for it?
Calling it personality when Scripture calls it sin?
Or am I bringing it into the light and submitting it to Christ?
James describes the terrifying progression:
“Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin…”
Notice the progression.
Desire.
Enticement.
Sin.
Death.
Sin rarely introduces itself by saying:
Hello. I am here to destroy you.
It usually says:
You need this.
You deserve this.
This will make the pain stop.
Nobody will know.
You can repent afterward.
It isn't really hurting anyone.
Everybody struggles with this.
And perhaps the oldest lie:
You can control it.
Until one day you realize the thing you thought you were holding has been holding you.
That is why Peter says these desires “wage war against your soul.”
War means you do not negotiate with what is trying to enslave you.
But Christianity is not merely a message telling desperate sinners to try harder.
If that were the Gospel, many of us would already be finished.
The Gospel says something infinitely better.
Jesus came for sinners.
Not polished sinners.
Not sinners who finally managed to make themselves presentable.
Sinners.
People with histories.
People with addictions.
People with hidden rooms.
People with ruined reputations.
People who knew better and did it anyway.
People who promised God and failed.
People carrying shame they cannot explain at church.
People whose private lives would scandalize the people sitting beside them on Sunday.
The cross does not tell us our sin was insignificant.
The cross tells us our sin was so serious that redemption cost the blood of Christ—and that God's grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly came to save sinners.
Paul says:
“Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.”
—Galatians 5:24
There is our word again.
Desires.
But notice what Christianity offers.
Not merely suppression.
Crucifixion.
And resurrection life.
You do not defeat the flesh simply by staring at the flesh all day.
You walk by the Spirit.
You behold Christ.
You bring darkness into light.
You repent.
You confess.
You remove opportunities for sin.
You renew your mind with Scripture.
You learn obedience.
You pursue Christian fellowship.
You remember whose you are.
And when you fall, you do not make peace with the ground.
You return to Jesus.
Because repentance is not pretending the fall never happened.
Repentance turns toward God.
The Hebrew Scriptures give us a beautiful word frequently associated with turning or returning:
שׁוּב — shuv
To turn back.
To return.
That picture matters.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible about yourself.
Judas experienced terrible remorse.
Repentance is a Godward turning.
You stop defending what Christ calls you to forsake.
You stop renaming darkness so you can comfortably keep it.
You stop asking how close you can live to sin without technically crossing a line.
You turn.
And you come home.
Perhaps somebody reading this has been hiding for years.
You love Jesus—or at least you desperately want to.
But there is a room inside you that you keep locked.
A browser history.
A relationship.
A habit.
A bottle.
A resentment.
A secret obsession.
A hunger for attention.
An emotional affair.
An ego.
An idol.
Something you would rather manage privately than surrender publicly before God.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows what is behind the door.
You are not protecting Him from the scandal.
You are hiding from grace.
And hiding is exhausting.
The Gospel invites you out.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Jesus matters more.
The cross means you never have to pretend sin is small in order to believe forgiveness is possible.
God can look directly at the ugliest truth about us and still point us toward the crucified and risen Christ.
John writes:
—1 John 1:9
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That does not make grace permission to continue rebelliously in sin. Paul destroys that idea in Romans 6.
Grace does not say:
Sin doesn't matter.
Grace says:
Sin will not have the final word over those who belong to Jesus.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear today.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church contained people with deeply sinful histories, yet after listing serious sins Paul could write these staggering words:
—1 Corinthians 6:11
Were.
There is a Gospel hidden inside that tense.
Your sin may describe where Christ found you.
It does not have the authority to decide who Christ can make you.
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified…”
That is scandalous grace.
Not grace that celebrates bondage.
Grace that breaks chains.
Not grace that teaches you to love darkness.
Grace that brings you into light.
Not grace that gives your flesh a more religious excuse.
Grace that teaches you to belong to Jesus.
This is why Romans 8:1 remains oxygen for ashamed believers:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation does not mean no conviction.
Conviction says:
Come out of this. Jesus has something better.
Condemnation says:
Stay hidden. God could never want you now.
Learn the difference.
The Holy Spirit exposes sin to lead us toward truth, repentance, holiness, and Christ.
Shame wants exposure to become your identity.
Jesus does not merely expose the scandal.
Jesus rewrites what happens after it.
Maybe tonight your prayer does not need impressive vocabulary.
Maybe it needs honesty.
Jesus, this desire has been controlling me.
I have called it weakness when sometimes I was choosing it.
I have hidden.
I have made excuses.
I cannot rescue myself.
Forgive me.
Clean me.
Teach me to walk by Your Spirit.
I belong to You.
That prayer is not a magic formula.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And Christianity is not behavior modification wrapped in religious vocabulary.
The center of Christianity is a Person.
Christ crucified.
Christ buried.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
Christ calling sinners to repentance and faith.
Christ giving His Spirit.
Christ transforming His people.
Christ coming again.
So what does the Bible mean by “passions of the flesh”?
It means more than sexual urges.
It means those desires shaped by fallen humanity that pull us toward life apart from God's will.
They can manifest as lust, greed, jealousy, rage, envy, selfish ambition, drunkenness, idolatry, rivalry, and countless other forms of disordered desire.
They promise satisfaction while waging war against the soul.
But they are not stronger than Jesus Christ.
The answer is not self-hatred.
The answer is not pretending you no longer experience temptation.
The answer is not religious performance.
The answer is surrender.
Walk by the Spirit.
Bring sin into the light.
Repent when you fall.
Believe the Gospel.
Feed what draws you toward Christ and starve what continually draws you away from Him.
And keep returning your eyes to Jesus.
Because the Christian life is not ultimately the story of how impressive your willpower became.
It is the story of how completely you learned that you needed a Savior.
If something in these words exposed something you have been hiding, don't rush away from that conviction.
Take it to Jesus.
And when you see somebody else saying those words, don't turn their vulnerability into gossip.
Pray for them.
We need Christian spaces where confession leads toward Christ rather than humiliation.
Send it privately to the believer who has grown tired.
Send it to the seeker who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
But whether you ever purchase anything or not, never confuse the invitation.
Jesus is not merchandise.
Grace is not for sale.
The blood of Christ cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
So share because somebody needs truth.
Tag because somebody you love may be hiding.
Save because tomorrow's temptation may try to make you forget today's conviction.
Follow because your soul needs more than an endless stream of noise.
But above everything else—
follow Jesus.
Because perhaps the desire you have been desperately protecting is actually the prison Christ is asking you to leave.
And perhaps the scandal you thought disqualified you forever is about to become the place where the world discovers just how astonishing the grace of Jesus Christ really is.
The flesh may remember your old appetites. The scars may remember your old battles. People may even remember your old name—but grace remembers who walked out of the tomb.
